strengths: Clear and well-motivated technical presentation: the inversion-free ODE formulation (Eqs. 2-3) is easy to follow, and the construction ensuring Z_src and Z_tar share the same noise instance so that common-noise components cancel in V_edit is well explained.

The two proposed components address real limitations of naively applying FlowEdit to video: SAFC provides an explicit, non-intrusive velocity-field masking mechanism with a concrete guarantee that non-edited regions remain frozen, and the ablation (Figure 5) directly visualizes the flow field with and without SAFC.

DAG is a practical efficiency contribution: Appendix D shows that 4-round differential guidance achieves results comparable to a 20-round averaging strategy, reducing a 41-frame edit from 29 minutes to 5 minutes on four 4090 GPUs, with a useful qualitative comparison.

Reasonably comprehensive quantitative evaluation across three video lengths (8/22/36 frames) with multiple metrics (Frame-Acc, Pick-Score, CLIP-T, CLIP-F, WarpSSIM, Qedit), plus honest discussion of the WarpSSIM result rather than hiding it, and a candid Limitation section (Figure 8 failure case, weak style-transfer performance).
Runs on a single consumer GPU and code is promised to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to FlowEdit: the core editing mechanism is a direct transposition of FlowEdit's velocity-difference ODE to the video/T2V setting. The most obvious baseline — FlowEdit applied directly to video with the same Wan 2.1 backbone, without SAFC/DAG — is conspicuously absent, so it is impossible to isolate how much of the reported gain comes from the proposed components versus simply using a much stronger T2V backbone.

The backbone confound undermines the headline SOTA claim: all five baselines (FateZero, FLATTEN, TokenFlow, RAVE, VideoDirector) are built on SD/T2I-era models, while FlowDirector uses the modern Wan 2.1 T2V model. Superior CLIP-T/Pick-Score numbers may largely reflect backbone quality rather than the editing framework; no backbone-controlled comparison or adaptation of a competing method to Wan is provided.

Evaluation set is self-curated: source videos are 'selected from the internet and generated by the Wan model.' Videos generated by the same backbone used by the proposed method plausibly favor it, and no standard benchmark (e.g., DAVIS-based editing suites used by prior work) or user study is reported, weakening external validity of the quantitative claims.

The DAG mechanism is heuristic and under-justified: the claim that the difference between a full-average and subset-average velocity estimate is a direction of 'improvement toward semantic alignment' analogous to CFG is asserted intuitively but never derived or theoretically supported. Its relationship to autoguidance [18] is acknowledged only as inspiration; ablations are purely qualitative for this component (no quantitative table isolating DAG's contribution).

SAFC's binary masks inherit the known brittleness of cross-attention localization (global-mean thresholding, sensitivity to block choice — the 18th DiT block is a manually chosen hyperparameter); behavior on multi-object, occluded, or large-motion scenes is not systematically evaluated, and there is no analysis of mask accuracy itself.

The WarpSSIM deficit is explained away qualitatively ('more substantial deformations'), but Table 2 shows the method is also worst on WarpL1/L2 for the single example analyzed; a broader analysis of the structure-preservation trade-off would be needed to accept this explanation at scale.

Some presentation issues: occasional typos ('Porscar', 'Rusult'), and several quantitative details (e.g., how Frame-Acc is computed, dataset size/number of edit prompts for Table 1) are underspecified in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: inversion-free, training-free text-to-video editing, which plausibly avoids known artifacts of inversion-based pipelines and is a direction of growing interest.

The method is clearly described end-to-end: the editing ODE (Eq. 3), the shared-noise construction of the target perturbed state, the SAFC masking procedure (including pseudocode in Algorithm 1 and hyperparameters in Appendix A/B), which supports reproducibility in principle.

Qualitative results are extensive (Figures 3, 4, 9-16), covering object replacement, texture change, attribute modification, addition/removal, and composite edits, and the ablation figures (5, 6, 7) give visual evidence that both SAFC and DAG contribute.
The paper is honest about the WarpSSIM result (Appendix C) and about failure modes (Appendix F, Figure 8), which is appreciated.
The comparison of DAG against a 20-round naive averaging strategy (Appendix D) provides a concrete efficiency argument (5 vs. 29 minutes on 4x4090 GPUs).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The core editing ODE with velocity differences over shared noise is a direct port of FlowEdit [24] from images to video with a new backbone (Wan 2.1). SAFC is essentially attention-map thresholding for masking, a very common technique in editing literature, applied to the velocity field; DAG is a CFG-like amplification of averaged velocity differences, which is a modest variation of FlowEdit's existing multi-noise averaging. The claimed contributions are therefore incremental on top of [24], and the paper's framing as 'a new paradigm' overstates the delta.

The central novelty claim ('the first work to apply the inversion-free editing paradigm to video') is not convincingly verified, and more importantly the most informative baseline is missing: FlowEdit itself adapted to video, or any other modern flow-based editing method. The comparisons are limited to FateZero, FLATTEN, TokenFlow, RAVE, and VideoDirector, all built on much older SD-based backbones.

The empirical gains are confounded by the base model. FlowDirector uses Wan 2.1 (1.3B, 2025) while all baselines use Stable-Diffusion-era models from 2023. The large CLIP-T and quality improvements likely reflect the stronger generative prior rather than the proposed components; without a same-backbone control, the SOTA claim is not well supported.

Evaluation breadth and rigor are limited. The evaluation set is self-curated ('videos selected from the internet and generated by the Wan model') with no public benchmark, no dataset/statistics description (number of videos, prompts, edit types), no human/user study, and metrics restricted to CLIP-based and warp-based proxies. The Q_edit metric is composite and non-standard. Ablations are almost entirely qualitative; there is no quantitative ablation table isolating SAFC and DAG on the reported metrics.

Computational cost is under-characterized. DAG requires 4 model passes per step plus the target/source passes, and Appendix D reports 5 minutes for a 41-frame video on four 4090 GPUs, which is substantial for a 'training-free' method; a fair cost comparison against baselines and against FlowEdit-with-averaging at matched budget is not provided in the main text.

Several design choices are presented heuristically without analysis: the fixed 18th DiT block for attention extraction, skipping the first 10 of 50 steps, the number of high-quality (4) and baseline (2) estimates, and the guidance weight w=2.75. Sensitivity analyses are absent, and it is unclear how fragile the method is across prompts, architectures, and mask quality (e.g., when cross-attention localization fails).

Presentation issues: recurring typos ('InsV2V' vs. FLATTEN reference, 'Rusult' in Figures 9-11, 'Porscar'), the related-work section does not engage with recent video editing methods built on modern backbones (e.g., CogVideoX- or VACE-based editing), and Figure 2's DAG panel is difficult to parse.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely problem: existing training-free video editing methods rely on inversion, which introduces temporal inconsistency and structural artifacts. Framing editing as a direct ODE-driven evolution in data space is a sensible alternative that avoids inversion errors entirely.

The proposed SAFC mechanism is well-motivated and technically clean: modulating the ODE velocity field to zero in non-target regions gives an explicit, model-external control over edit locality, in contrast to prior attention-replacement tricks that intervene inside the network. The ablation in Figure 5 (editing flow visualization with/without SAFC) provides direct evidence that the mechanism concentrates the flow on the target region.

DAG is supported by a useful ablation (Appendix D, Figure 7) comparing it against naive multi-round averaging, showing comparable quality at roughly 6x lower compute (4 vs. 20 inference rounds). This is the right baseline to compare against for a guidance-style averaging scheme.

Quantitative evaluation is broader than typical: six metrics across three video lengths (8/22/36 frames), and the paper is commendably transparent about not winning every metric (WarpSSIM), with a plausible explanation in Appendix C.

The limitations section is honest and specific (incomplete prompt replacement failures in Figure 8, weak style transfer), and the appendix provides enough implementation detail (mask smoothing window, feathering decay, CFG scales, block choice) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core editing trajectory (Eqs. 2-3) is a direct adaptation of FlowEdit [24] from images to video. The paper acknowledges this dependency, which weakens the headline claim of a 'new paradigm.' The genuinely new components (SAFC, DAG) are relatively incremental: SAFC is a velocity-field masking scheme built from standard cross-attention maps, and DAG is closely related to the multi-noise averaging that FlowEdit already performs — the paper needs a sharper technical differentiation of DAG from FlowEdit's averaging, since both compute expectations of the velocity difference over noise samples.

There is a significant confound in the baseline comparison: FlowDirector is built on Wan 2.1, a much stronger modern T2V foundation model, while most compared baselines (FateZero, FLATTEN, TokenFlow, RAVE) are built on substantially older image-diffusion backbones. Superior CLIP-T, PickScore, and temporal metrics may largely reflect the stronger generative prior rather than the editing algorithm. At least one baseline using a comparable backbone (e.g., VideoDirector, or an inversion-based method on Wan) with matched capacity is needed to attribute the gains to the method.

The evaluation set is self-curated ('videos selected from the internet and generated by the Wan model') with no standard benchmark (e.g., DAVIS-based protocols used by TokenFlow/RAVE), no user study, and no stated sample size or selection protocol. This raises cherry-picking concerns, particularly since CLIP-based metrics are known to be gameable and correlate imperfectly with human judgment of edit quality.

Ablations in the main text (Figures 5-6) are purely qualitative; there are no quantitative ablation numbers (e.g., metrics with/without SAFC and DAG) to substantiate the magnitude of each component's contribution.

DAG adds multi-pass inference per denoising step (4 forward passes), but computational cost is only reported late in the appendix and not in the main experiments table, making efficiency claims ('reducing computational overhead') hard to verify. The method also inherits sensitivity to architecture-specific choices (e.g., '18th DiT block') whose selection heuristic is not rigorously justified.
Code is only promised, not released, which limits reproducibility assessment at review time.
